I'm a quality engineer at a car plant near Stuttgart, and last winter we had a strange problem. Some brake parts from one of our suppliers were failing our tests, but only on Monday mornings. At first, we thought the parts might have been damaged during transport. Then we checked the trucks, and they were fine, so the transport can't have been the problem. We asked for the production records, and we saw something interesting. On Mondays, the furnace had been off for the whole weekend. The first parts of the week must have been cast while the metal was still too cold. The supplier changed the start-up procedure, and the problem disappeared. My lesson from that case is simple. Look at the data first, and only then decide who is guilty.

I manage supplier quality for a tractor company in Pune. Two years ago, a customer sent back a whole container of engine parts. Every part had small holes inside the metal. The supplier said the problem couldn't have started in their plant, because their process had not changed in ten years. So I went there myself. It was the middle of the monsoon, and the sand storage area had no roof. I said, the rain must have got into the sand. The manager wasn't happy, but he agreed to run a test. We dried the sand, and the holes disappeared. Since then, I always ask one question first. What changed? Sometimes it isn't the machine or the people. Sometimes it's just the weather.

In my job as a consultant, I often arrive at a factory after something has gone wrong. And the first thing I hear is usually a name. It must have been the night shift, someone says. Or, he can't have followed the instructions. I always stop that conversation. When a part fails, people want someone to blame, but blame never fixes a process. So we start with facts. Which batch was it? When was it made? Which machine, which material, which operator? Very often the answer surprises everyone. The night shift might have made the parts, but the real cause was a change in the material that nobody had noticed. Find the cause, fix the process, and leave the names out of it.
